segments.text: This is one of the best-known images of American history: Washington Crossing the Delaware. On a winter river, among floating ice, George Washington stands in a small boat and looks ahead. Behind him, a soldier raises the Stars and Stripes. But this painting was not made in seventeen seventy-six. It was made about seventy-five years later, in Germany. And on the night of the crossing, that flag had not yet been adopted as the nation's flag.
In this episode, we follow the image through time: from a winter night on the river, to a painter's studio in Düsseldorf, to the city where the painting became famous.

On the evening of December twenty-fifth, seventeen seventy-six, Washington's army began to cross the Delaware River, from Pennsylvania into New Jersey, on its way to Trenton. Two days later, Washington described the crossing in a letter to John Hancock, the president of Congress.

The plan was to start as soon as it grew dark. But ice formed in the river that night, and slowed the boats so much that it was three o'clock before all the artillery was across, and nearly four before the troops began to march. He called it a very severe night, and wrote that they marched through a violent storm of snow and hail.

In the painting, a morning light is spreading across the sky, and a last star still shines above the boat. Studies of the painting connect this light with the coming dawn. The crossing that went on through the night is gathered here into a single view.

The flag in the painting has red and white stripes, and white stars on a blue field. This is the Stars and Stripes. On June fourteenth, seventeen seventy-seven, about six months after the crossing, the Continental Congress resolved that the flag of the United States would have thirteen stripes and thirteen stars. The resolution did not say how the stars should be arranged. Which flag was carried that night, if any, is not known.

The painter, Emanuel Leutze, was born in Germany in eighteen sixteen. As a child, he moved with his family to the United States. In eighteen forty-one, he went back to Germany to study painting, in Düsseldorf, a city known for its painters of history.

He began the first version of this picture there in eighteen forty-nine, soon after revolutions swept across Europe in eighteen forty-eight. Mount Vernon, Washington's home and now a museum, explains that Leutze supported those revolutions, and hoped his painting would inspire new struggles for liberty and democracy.

Americans in the city posed for the figures. One of them, the painter Worthington Whittredge, recalled that he posed for the man steering the boat, and again for Washington himself. For Washington's head, Leutze is said to have looked to a sculpture by Houdon.

In November eighteen fifty, a fire in the studio damaged the first version. The next year, Leutze began a second one. The first was repaired, went to the city of Bremen, and was lost in an air raid in nineteen forty-two.

In eighteen fifty-one, the second version was shown in New York, and crowds came to see it. Two years later, an engraving after the painting was published, carrying the image far beyond the exhibition room.
In eighteen ninety-seven, it was given to the Metropolitan Museum of Art, where it hangs today. It is more than six meters wide.

So, did Washington really cross the Delaware like this? The painting was made about seventy-five years after the night it shows, in another country. Its painter put the light of morning in the sky, and the later flag of a nation in a soldier's hands. It is not a record of that night. It is a picture of that night, made for the painter's own time. And today, it is the picture that many of us remember.
Every story has an origin. Sometimes, the image we remember was painted long after the moment itself.
